The judge is looking for every indicator on the list, whether or not their own questions reach it. If the conversation never reaches one, steer your answer there and show the idea working. While you plan, get one workable line on each before you make any of them longer.

Two indicators on one topic are still two jobs. “Describe the refund policy” and “Apply it to this customer’s request” ask for different things.

A budget or a staffing limit shapes how you show an indicator. A limit like that is not itself an indicator.

misconception.wrongModel: If I say the indicator out loud, or mention its topic, I have covered it.
misconception.whyItFails: Repeating the wording shows you can read. An answer that names every indicator and shows none has shown none.
misconception.betterModel: It is covered when someone who never saw your card could hear your answer and tell you understood the idea and used it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping at a definition when the indicator says demonstrate.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Describing how you would calm an unhappy customer is not calming the one the judge is playing.
commonMistakes.fix: When the verb asks for an action, plan the moment the judge watches.

commonMistakes.mistake: Doing brilliant work on something that was not listed.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Extra strength makes the meeting better. It still cannot stand in for a listed skill.
commonMistakes.fix: Reach every listed indicator first. Then give your remaining time to the weakest one.

name: Healthcare Ethics
description: Make responsible choices using safety, privacy, and respect.

lesson.title: Reason through healthcare ethics
lesson.summary: Use privacy, consent, safety, and fairness to evaluate scenarios.

content.objective: Use ethical principles to choose a safe and respectful response.
content.explanation: Healthcare ethics often involves balancing values like privacy, patient choice, safety, and professional responsibility.
content.whyMatters: HOSA scenarios may test what you do when the easy answer is not the most responsible answer.
steps: Identify the people affected.
Name the ethical issue.
Choose the safest professional action.
Explain why it respects the patient.

workedExample.prompt: A friend asks about a patient's condition.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Tell them if they promise not to share.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I cannot share private patient information. I would direct them to the proper contact process and protect confidentiality.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer protects privacy and gives a professional next step.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which principle is involved when protecting patient information?
choices: Privacy
Marketing
Weighing
Pricing
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Privacy
guidedQuestion.hint: Think about information access.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Patient information should be protected unless sharing is authorized.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should you do with private patient information?
choices: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
Tell friends
Post it
Guess publicly
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
practiceQuestions.hint: Privacy rules matter.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Professional ethics requires protecting patient information.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is an ethical response?
choices: Respect patient dignity
Ignore consent
Embarrass the patient
Skip safety
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Respect patient dignity
practiceQuestions.hint: Ethics centers people.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Respecting dignity supports professional care.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why explain your ethical choice?
choices: To show reasoning and professionalism
To make it longer only
To avoid action
To confuse the judge
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To show reasoning and professionalism
practiceQuestions.hint: Judges need to see your decision process.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explaining the principle makes the answer stronger.

masteryCheck.prompt: A scenario involves risk of harm. What principle becomes urgent?
choices: Safety
Advertising
Speaker rank
Budget
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Safety
masteryCheck.hint: Health scenarios prioritize harm reduction.
masteryCheck.explanation: Safety is central when someone could be harmed.

name: Medical Terminology Basics
description: Break clinical words into roots, prefixes, and suffixes.

lesson.title: Decode medical terms
lesson.summary: Use word parts to understand unfamiliar health terms.

content.objective: Break medical terms into word parts and explain them accurately.
content.explanation: Many medical terms are built from prefixes, roots, and suffixes. If you can identify parts, you can understand unfamiliar terms more safely.
content.whyMatters: HOSA events reward accurate health science language. Terminology also helps you communicate clearly with patients and judges.
steps: Find the prefix.
Find the root.
Find the suffix.
Put the meaning together and check context.

workedExample.prompt: Tachycardia
workedExample.weakAnswer: A heart problem.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Tachy means fast and cardia relates to the heart, so tachycardia means a fast heart rate.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer uses word parts and avoids vague guessing.

guidedQuestion.prompt: In tachycardia, what does tachy mean?
choices: Fast
Slow
Lung
Skin
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Fast
guidedQuestion.hint: Think of tachometer: speed.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Tachy means fast.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What does cardi relate to?
choices: Heart
Liver
Bone
Skin
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Heart
practiceQuestions.hint: Cardiology studies the heart.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cardi/cardio refers to the heart.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why use word parts?
choices: To infer meaning safely
To diagnose without context
To avoid communication
To skip definitions
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To infer meaning safely
practiceQuestions.hint: Word parts are clues, not the whole clinical picture.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Word parts help decode terms while still respecting context.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is most precise?
choices: Tachycardia means fast heart rate
Tachycardia is bad stuff
Tachycardia is always fatal
Tachycardia means slow breathing
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Tachycardia means fast heart rate
practiceQuestions.hint: Avoid exaggeration.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This answer is accurate and appropriately limited.

masteryCheck.prompt: What does hypo usually mean?
choices: Low or under
High
Heart
Bone
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Low or under
masteryCheck.hint: Hypo means below.
masteryCheck.explanation: Hypo often means low, under, or deficient.

name: Patient Communication
description: Explain health information clearly, respectfully, and safely.

lesson.title: Communicate with patients clearly
lesson.summary: Use empathy, plain language, and confirmation checks.

content.objective: Explain health information in plain language and confirm understanding.
content.explanation: Patient communication combines accuracy and empathy. A strong response avoids jargon, listens to concerns, and checks understanding.
content.whyMatters: In healthcare, communication affects safety. Patients need to understand next steps, risks, and when to ask for help.
steps: Acknowledge the concern.
Explain in plain language.
Give the next step.
Ask a teach-back question.

workedExample.prompt: A patient is nervous about a blood pressure reading.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Your systolic is elevated; just calm down.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I understand this number can feel stressful. Blood pressure can change for many reasons, so we will recheck it and share it with the provider. Can you tell me what step we are taking next?
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer is empathetic, clear, and checks understanding.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which response best uses plain language?
choices: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
Your systolic parameter requires clinical correlation.
Do not worry about it.
This is definitely a diagnosis.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: We will recheck your blood pressure and talk with the provider.
guidedQuestion.hint: Plain language is accurate and understandable.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This response avoids jargon and gives a safe next step.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is teach-back?
choices: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
Repeating jargon faster
Ignoring questions
Giving a diagnosis
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Asking the patient to explain the next step in their own words
practiceQuestions.hint: It checks understanding.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Teach-back helps confirm the patient understands.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which tone is best?
choices: Calm and respectful
Dismissive
Sarcastic
Rushed
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Calm and respectful
practiceQuestions.hint: Healthcare communication needs trust.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A calm tone supports professionalism and patient safety.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why avoid jargon?
choices: Patients may not understand it
It is always illegal
It makes answers shorter
It replaces accuracy
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Patients may not understand it
practiceQuestions.hint: Communication is about understanding.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Plain language improves comprehension without sacrificing accuracy.

masteryCheck.prompt: A patient says they are confused. What should you do?
choices: Pause and explain again in simpler language
Move on immediately
Use more abbreviations
Ignore the concern
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Pause and explain again in simpler language
masteryCheck.hint: Respond to the concern.
masteryCheck.explanation: Clear communication includes adapting when the patient is confused.

name: Evidence-Based Reasoning
description: Support claims with examples, reasoning, and responsible evidence.

lesson.title: Support your message with evidence
lesson.summary: Make speeches more credible with support and explanation.

content.objective: Use evidence and reasoning to support a public speaking claim.
content.explanation: Evidence can be an example, data point, expert idea, or personal story. Reasoning explains how the evidence proves the claim.
content.whyMatters: Audiences are more likely to trust a message when they can see why it is true.
steps: State the claim.
Give specific support.
Explain the connection.
Tie it back to the audience.

workedExample.prompt: Claim: practice improves confidence.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Practice is obviously helpful.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Practice improves confidence because repeated rehearsal makes the speech feel familiar. For example, a student who practices the opening five times is less likely to freeze when starting.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer gives reasoning and a concrete example.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What does reasoning do?
choices: Explains how evidence proves the claim
Starts the timer
Removes examples
Changes the topic
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Explains how evidence proves the claim
guidedQuestion.hint: Reasoning is the bridge.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Reasoning connects support to the claim.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is evidence?
choices: A specific example
A vague feeling only
No support
A transition word
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A specific example
practiceQuestions.hint: Evidence supports a claim.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Examples can function as evidence when they prove a point.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why explain evidence?
choices: So the audience understands its meaning
To make it confusing
To avoid claims
To skip the conclusion
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: So the audience understands its meaning
practiceQuestions.hint: Do not make listeners infer everything.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explanation turns evidence into persuasion.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is strongest?
choices: Practice helps because familiarity reduces fear at the start.
Practice good.
I like practice.
No one needs examples.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Practice helps because familiarity reduces fear at the start.
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for claim plus why.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This answer gives a reason that supports the claim.

masteryCheck.prompt: A story supports your point only if you also do what?
choices: Explain the connection
Hide the claim
Skip the audience
Use no structure
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Explain the connection
masteryCheck.hint: Evidence needs interpretation.
masteryCheck.explanation: The speaker must show how the story proves the message.

name: Presentation Structure
description: Organize speeches with a clear opening, body, and close.

lesson.title: Structure a clear speech
lesson.summary: Build a speech listeners can follow from start to finish.

content.objective: Use a simple structure: hook, thesis, main points, and close.
content.explanation: Strong speeches feel easy to follow because each part has a job. The opening earns attention, the thesis states the message, the body proves it, and the close makes it memorable.
content.whyMatters: Structure lowers anxiety and helps audiences remember your message.
steps: Start with a hook.
State the thesis.
Organize two or three main points.
Close by returning to the main message.

workedExample.prompt: Speech about why students should learn public speaking.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Public speaking is good and helps people.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Have you ever had a great idea but felt too nervous to say it? Public speaking helps students turn ideas into action. I will show how it builds confidence, clarity, and leadership.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer has a hook, thesis, and preview.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What does a thesis do?
choices: States the main message
Ends the timer
Adds a random example
Replaces the body
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: States the main message
guidedQuestion.hint: The thesis tells the audience what the speech argues.
guidedQuestion.explanation: A thesis gives the speech direction.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What belongs in the opening?
choices: Hook and thesis
Only citations
No topic
A hidden conclusion
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Hook and thesis
practiceQuestions.hint: Openings orient listeners.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The opening should earn attention and state the message.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why use two or three main points?
choices: They are easier to remember
They make the speech endless
They avoid structure
